The Life ReviewPatina Designer Portal · 28 Aug 2026

    A UI review of the designer portal · Patina

    The Life Review

    The portal is not broken. It is one paper, one rule and one size, wherever you look — and three ways to change that without moving a single thing.

    Three directions, named plainly and never mixed together on one page:

    • A — Ink on Paper. A real type scale and a three-weight rule system.
    • B — Honest Materials. Tint by document movement, filled status, product imagery.
    • C — The Dark Desk. The paper as a sheet laid on a dark desk.
    Provenance
    Fresh captures 2026-08-28 · local seed · UI only
    Scope
    Tokens, type, rules, grounds, fills, imagery, chrome tone
    Standing note
    Nothing here changes a route, an act, a label or a workflow

    THE ASK

    What was asked, and how we read it

    “You are a senior UI designer, Review the current designer portal and make recommendations to bring more life to the page, designers are complaining it is too flat and everything blends together. Only suggest UI improvements and dont change the UX or workflow. Present three optinos in an HTML presentation for the Patina team to weigh in on.”

    Reproduced verbatim, spelling included.

    How we read it

    “UI-only” means tokens, type, rule weights, grounds, fills, imagery and chrome tone. It does not mean routes, acts, copy or information architecture — every one of those stays exactly as it stands today.

    What a direction is here

    A direction is a token-delta table over the real globals.css, a set of component recipes so the cost is honest, and mockups drawn on the same specimen data in every lane — never a new layout, never a new act.

    How the evidence was made

    Fresh 1440 and 390 captures of the current build, taken 2026-08-28 against local seed data, signed in as designer Leah Hartwell. A measurement script read every visible element's computed style off the rendered DOM. One audit seat — a simulated designer's eye, said plainly wherever it speaks — walked the captures against those numbers. Priors already on record from four earlier reviews are folded in with their file and line.

    The two rulings already taken

    • A lean pipeline built this deck, not the full house review process.
    • A bounded shadow amendment to canon D4 is asked only as a question, later in this deck — no mockup here shows a shadow, and no direction depends on one.
    Standing disclosure

    This deck rests on one simulated seat and measured numbers, not customer research. The desk capture reads from local seed data, not a production account.

    FINDINGS

    Twenty-five findings, four of them blockers

    Twenty-five findings came out of the walk: four blocker, eleven high, nine medium, one low. By theme, type carries seven, tone five, state four, chrome four, color two, material two, rule one. Every fix is a token, a type step, a rule weight, a fill, a ground or a crop — nothing that moves a route, a label or an act.

    No dedicated finding-card class exists in 00-head.html; the cards below reuse .q-card (the question-card kit), which already carries an id line, a title and a meta row.

    PLANKS

    Nine planks, and no direction skips one

    A plank is a repair the surface needs whichever direction the team rules for — a token, a floor, a fill or a ground. “No plank adds a surface, moves a region, changes a label, or changes what any act does” (shared-planks.md). Where a direction restates a plank at its own value — Direction A's stocks are deeper, so A's inks are one step darker — the plank is still adopted, never replaced.

    • SP-01

      A 14px body floor and an 11px mono floor

      F11 F12 F13 F14 F21 F22

      Every text-bearing element on a Document surface lands on one of five steps — mono label 11px, mono state 12px, body 14px, name 16px, head 18px+ — so --type-body-min: 14px and --type-metadata-min: 12px become the floor in fact instead of a suggestion beside it, and the mono floor moves to 11px because 649 of 1,029 mono usages (63%) already sit at or below 10px, 296 of them at exactly 9px. The tokens are the easy part: text-[<n>px] literals run 1,749 deep across 252 files in 25 distinct sizes, and the seven named components are where the decisions are, not where the work is.

      Size L · its own lane, 4–6 days, sequenced before any direction ships · globals.css · 1,749 text-[<n>px] literals across 252 files in components/document/**

    • SP-02

      Three muted inks that are three colours

      F16

      --text-muted, --text-subtle and --text-faint all resolve to #65594E today; they become three steps — --text-muted: #4E4339, --text-subtle: #5A4E43, --text-faint: #65594E kept at today's value as the quietest step — and all three clear 4.5:1 on every ground any direction declares.

      Size S · globals.css only

    • SP-03

      A rule-weight token set, and one job per weight

      F18

      Three tokens replace the single pearl hairline used 502 times: --rule-hair for a row ended, --rule-mid for a section ended, --rule-double (the existing .doc-region-rule) for a movement ended — one weight per rank instead of one weight carrying all three.

      All three are hardcoded charcoal, so any inverted chrome erases them: on Direction C's three charcoals — desk #37322D, rails #2C2926, well #201D1B — --rule-mid reads 1.141 / 1.000 / 1.159 and --rule-hair reads 1.015 / 1.000 / 1.011, on the rails literally the ground's own colour. The plank owns a dark twin for each weight, spent only by a lane that inverts a ground — today that is C alone, and C prices them.

    • SP-06

      Hover is the next stock the lane already declares

      F17 F01

      --bg-hover moves off rgba(196,165,123,.06) — 1.042:1 over the ground — but it is a rule now, not a hex: a hovered row takes the next stock the direction already declared for that lane, because one value could not clear 1.10:1 across every stock every direction proposes. The one hex this plank tried, --plank-hover-tint: #F3ECE2, measured 1.008–1.125:1 across the declared stocks and inverted direction on two of them — 1.228:1 on A's desk (lighter than the ground) and 1.089:1 on B's rail (also lighter) — and a fill deep enough to clear 1.10:1 everywhere else broke SP-04's floor: charcoal at 6% over A's desk stock reads 1.106:1 and drops A's tightest -ink to 4.137:1 on the hovered row; over B's Project stock, 1.115:1 and 4.363:1. So the plank promises a floor of at least 1.09:1, not 1.10:1, and the floor is 1.097 — C's second sheet, the tightest value any lane's rule produces. Every lane clears it with a stock it already owns: A takes the rail stock (paper · rail · desk — 1.177 · 1.177 · 1.173), B takes the untinted sheet showing through the tint (1.108–1.116 on the six stocks, 1.225 on the rail), C takes the second sheet on paper and the next charcoal on the chrome (1.097 · 1.141 · 1.159). The FF&E row's own local 4% hover is deleted in favour of the rule.

    DIRECTION A · Ink on Paper

    Direction A — Ink on Paper

    The portal already has one good idea about hierarchy — set it in type, on paper, with a rule — and it never commits to it. Playfair runs at thirty-nine sizes and tops out at 27.9px on a document; three quarters of the small type sits under the reading floor; one pearl hairline ends a row, a section and a chapter alike; and the three grounds that name three places sit inside 1.07:1.

    A takes the existing grammar literally. On top of the planks every lane adopts, A adds three paper stocks 1.18:1 apart, a five-step Playfair scale, four one-step-darker inks, and one device that opens every section: the Strata mark, a mono label, a Playfair name, a 1.5px charcoal rule. No new colour, no imagery, no inversion.

    The plank block ships with every lane: the reading floor, three muted inks, three rule weights, the state fill and the hover step are shared by A, B and C, and the figures below already carry them. What is A's alone is the section head, the three stocks and the type scale laid on top.

    What stays identical

    Every route, component, act, label and piece of information architecture. The desk still opens on “Good morning, Leah”, the same three acts with the same sub-labels, the same whisper notes, the same roster under “EVERY JOB · 16 LIVE · 1 OVERDUE” grouped by the same stages in the same order, the same studio index, the same drawer with the same five doorways. The document keeps its spine, paper, margin, letterhead, red-letter zone, region heads and their ledgers of acts, and its FF&E lines by room. Nothing folds that did not fold; nothing moves surface; no word changes. A is a stylesheet.

    The risk taken

    The desk stops being white. The desk route's ground goes from #FAF7F2 to #E0D6C4 — a warm tan 1.381:1 under the document paper. It is the single move that makes putting a document down feel like putting it down, and it is also the move a team can reject on sight: for three years the portal has been one cream. If the ground is refused, the rest of A still stands — the scale, the rules, the section head — and the two rail stocks alone still open the document's three columns.

    Recipes by surface

    Desk ground & roster
    The stock is #E0D6C4, scoped to the desk route; the roster prints straight on it, one line per job, never a card, the job name 16px to 18px.
    Document paper
    Unchanged at #FCFAF6; the title goes to 40px and the letterhead closes with the mid rule, not a pearl hairline.
    Section heads & rules
    The signature: Strata mark at 40/28/16px by 2px, a mono 11px label, a 24px Playfair name, then the mid rule across the measure; the double rule only at movement rank.
    Spine
    Ground #EFE7DA, so the left column reads as a column; the in-hand box takes the rail's hairline and stops outweighing the four places the document goes.
    Margin
    The spine's stock, so the paper is flanked by one material on both sides; the chip's eyebrow goes from 8px to mono 11px.
    Drawer
    Ground #FCFAF6 — the paper stock, not white — with the mid rule along its top edge, the one place in A that rule runs the window's full width.
    Status & stamps
    The chip keeps its dot and word at mono 11px in --text-faint; the stamp keeps its outline and rotation and wears the planks' fill for the state that put the row there.
    FF&E lines
    Name and price both at 15px, so the number stops outranking the piece, and the maker rises to the mono floor.
    Red-letter zone
    The fill becomes a declared stock at 1.220:1 under the sheet, the left edge stays 2px terracotta, the eyebrow keeps its ink at 5.18:1.
    390
    Nothing in A depends on width: the stocks, the scale and the rules hold at one column, and the mobile bar is the charcoal strip it already is.

    Findings addressed

    The planks close F11, F12, F13, F14, F21, F22 (SP-01), F16, F18, F02, F03, F01, F17, F06, F07, F08 and F24 in all three lanes. What A closes on its own:

    F05 Room, paper and card sit inside 1.07 to 1 F09 The most urgent band is the palest band F10 A section head and a state chip are one style F11 Playfair has thirty-nine sizes and no scale F13 The desk's type gives the work no rank F14 On a furniture line the price outranks the piece

    A brings no imagery and no texture and does not touch People, so F15, F19, F20 and F25 stay open, as does F02's shape half: the dot still carries five states, and A only makes the ink under it legible.

    Canon check

    • D4, five lint selectors: none tripped. Every A move is a token value, a font-size, a border-width or a border-colour; the stylesheet and all four A fragments grep clean for shadows.
    • D1: untouched. A moves no surface, opens no panel, adds no tab.
    • Typography-first: A is nothing but type, colour and rule weight, and its section device is the Strata mark, which is what the app's own guidance names for the role.
    • Never a card: the roster stays list lines, and moving --doc-surface off pure white makes cards less card-like, not more.
    • The contrast test: A's inks move downward in luminance and clear the floor everywhere — 20 pairs, zero failures, lowest 4.577. The edit is three stocks added, plus the red-letter entry re-derived, against a hardcoded list of five grounds rather than one array. white: '#FFFFFF' stays valid and load-bearing: 108 bg-white literals inside components/document still paint it, and after the scoping it is the ratio that protects them.

    Keeps · Refuses · Costs

    Keeps
    The paper. The Scored Ink grammar and its one inked leader. The Strata mark as the section device. Every route, act, label and region, in place and in order.
    Refuses
    No colour beyond the four inks it darkens. No tint by state or movement, no imagery, no texture, no inversion, no second mark shape for state. It does not ask for the amendment.
    Scope
    The tan ground is scoped to the desk route, not to --bg-primary, which is what the route shell paints under every document route — repointing that would take Library, People and every ledger sheet with it. The scoping is one component edit; repointing instead costs two to three more days and three rooms to draw first. A's second app-wide token is scoped the same way: --bg-surface becomes a --doc-surface declared on the Document tree, because var(--bg-surface) resolves 83 times across 51 files — scope-builder, procurement, proposals, FF&E, the shared controls, the toast provider, the mood board — and repointing it at the root repaints every white surface in the portal shell. Both scopings are what make A's “does not touch People, Library or the ledger layouts” true.
    Costs
    A's own work is two to three days: about twenty token edits, eleven named components and two scoping edits. It rides on two sweeps that belong to the planks and are not in that figure — 1,749 text-[<n>px] literals across 252 files, and 502 border-[var(--color-pearl)] literals across 172. Reversibility is high: every value is a token.

    DIRECTION B · Honest Materials

    Direction B — Honest Materials

    A designer's day is spent judging things by eye, and across twenty-two captures the portal shows no piece of furniture, no fabric, no finish and no room. It also spends six named phase hues on nothing but a folder tab.

    B puts both to work. Paper is tinted by the movement the document is in — one stock per stage group the desk prints, drawn from the six shipped --phase-* hues and tuned against the ground each is painted on. Status stops being a hue on a 6px dot and becomes a filled stamp with its matching ink. The letterhead and the red-letter zone share one charcoal band. Where an FF&E line links a catalog product, a 48px thumbnail sits on it.

    What stays identical

    Every route, component, act, label and piece of information architecture. The desk opens on “Good morning, Leah” with the same three acts and whisper notes; the roster keeps “EVERY JOB · 16 LIVE · 1 OVERDUE”, the same stage groups in the same order, one line per job, never a card; the studio index keeps its labels and doorways with no counts; the drawer keeps its five doorways. The document keeps its spine, paper, margin, letterhead, red-letter zone, region heads and their ledgers, and its FF&E lines by room. The tab is the movement word the surface already prints; the tint is the stock that word is printed on.

    The risk taken

    The charcoal band. The letterhead and the red-letter zone sit together on #2C2926, bled to the paper's edge — the first opaque dark block the document has carried, and the highest-contrast object on the page at 12.485:1 against the Project stock the sheet takes — 13.87:1 is the figure for an untinted sheet, and B tints every document. It answers the palest-band finding with the bluntest instrument in the box, and it is the move most likely to read as an app rather than a document. It is reversible in one token: drop the band, keep the tints, and B is quieter but intact.

    Token deltas that matter

    Each stock against the ground it is painted on, then the sheet. Every hex is its --phase-* hue composited over the sheet #FCFAF6 and measured against the ground #FAF7F2 — composite over the ground instead and you get six different colours.

    The rail is the correction this draft owes. Deepening the stocks by about 8% ate the rail's headroom and the earlier rail was not re-measured: at #ECE7DF it read 1.058 to 1.066 against the six sheets it actually flanks — every one below today's 1.081, so B was the one lane whose rails went backwards — while the findings table advertised 1.152 against the desk ground, which the rails never touch in either view. The rail is now #E8E3DB, at 1.098 to 1.106 against all six and 1.225 under the untinted sheet. The price is exact and it is not free: on that rail three of the four paper inks fall under the 4.5 floor — golden hour 4.452, terracotta 4.414, sage 4.411 — so B's rail carries only charcoal, the three muted inks and clay ink at 4.697, the token is declared as a quiet stock, and the rail cannot join the contrast test's ground list. There is no third option: 1.08 under the deepest sheet caps the rail at a relative luminance of 0.7858, and sage ink needs 0.7886.

    What the stocks do and do not do. They carry value against the ground — 1.081 to 1.088, against the 1.025 this deck calls the defect — and hue against each other. They do not carry value against each other: all six sit one step above the same ground, so pairwise they measure 1.000 to 1.007. Two are costs rather than wins: Brief reaches 1.088 only at 13% of a cool hue and arrives a near-neutral grey, the one cool surface in a warm system; Project needs 22% of golden hour and arrives a buff manila, which on the document is the whole sheet.

    Recipes by surface

    Desk ground & roster
    The ground stays #FAF7F2; each stage group is a band of its own stock, bled to the page's edges so it has no edge, under a saturated tab of the same hue.
    Document paper
    The sheet takes the movement's stock; the letterhead sits on the band with the movement's tab above the title.
    Section heads & rules
    The planks' three weights, the section rule taking the movement's tab pigment instead of charcoal.
    Spine
    #E8E3DB, one step under every stock — 1.098 to 1.106 below the six, 1.225 below the untinted sheet, against today's 1.081. It does not go deeper because it is already past the point where three of the four paper inks hold 4.5:1 on it.
    Margin
    The rail stock; the chips keep the sheet's paper as their fill, so a note reads as paper laid on the rail.
    Drawer
    The sheet's paper with a 16%-charcoal top edge, distinct from a card, which is now a tinted stock, not white.
    Filled states
    In every figure here the fill lands on the stamp, not the chip: StatusChip has no reachable render on this data. The stamp's 1.5px pigment border stays and does the separating.
    FF&E lines
    A 48px thumbnail leads a line only where it links a catalog product; where none does, the line keeps the slot at the rail stock, 1.103 under the Project sheet — a material, not a blank.
    Red-letter zone
    On the band: base terracotta for the label at 6.36:1, off-white for the row at 13.53:1.
    390
    The stocks and tabs carry the stage groups once the acts stack, which makes this the width where B is most exposed.

    Findings addressed

    The planks close the reading floor, the muted inks, the rule weights, hover, the drawer, the rails and the fourth ground in all three lanes. What B closes on its own:

    F15 Nothing shows what is bought F09 F02 F03 F20 F25

    B does not restate the type scale, so F11, F13 and F14 are closed only to the planks' floors. F05 is closed in part: the sheet is tinted and the rails open to 1.098 to 1.106 against the sheets they flank, but the desk ground is unchanged. People is untouched.

    Canon check

    • D4, five lint selectors: none tripped. Every B move is a background colour, a border colour, a background image or a repeating gradient.
    • D1: untouched. The tab is a label's treatment, not a control; it opens nothing.
    • Typography-first: B leans least on type, which is a fair charge. Its defence is that the rule bans cards-within-cards and tab bars as the mechanism, not colour; B adds no nesting and no bar.
    • Never a card: the band bleeds to the page's own edges — no left edge, no right edge, no radius — so it is a stock the lines are printed on. An earlier draft had a radius and stopped short of the edges, and read as a panel. The tab still reads as a label plate rather than a notched folder tab at deck scale; that is not answered here.
    • The contrast test: the four ink values are unchanged; the ground list gains the six stocks and the five fills — 108 pairs, zero failures, the tightest sage ink and terracotta ink on the damaged fill at 4.626 and 4.629 — and not the rail, which three of the four inks do not clear. An earlier draft printed the floor as 5.52 on the rail; the binding pair there was 4.578, and the rail move is what puts the floor back on the damaged fill, where the paragraph protecting it already is.

    Keeps · Refuses · Costs

    Keeps
    The paper as reading surface. One line per job. The six phase hues the product already names. Every route, act, label and region in place and in order.
    Refuses
    No type-scale change beyond the planks' floors. No inverted chrome. No photograph where a catalog link does not exist, and no room scan shown as a picture. No badge, count or tile. It does not ask for the amendment.
    The open number
    How many production FF&E lines carry a product_id. Locally it is zero of six, with 21 catalog products of which 17 have images — so on this data B's headline move renders no thumbnails, and the two crops in the figure are stood in to show the treatment. Nobody in this program has the production figure. Ask for it before ruling: if it is near zero, B's answer to F15 is aspirational and should be read that way.
    Costs
    Four to six days of B's own work, plus the planks. One thing the tokens cannot hold for you: the rail's register — charcoal, the muted ramp and clay ink on the rail, the warm pigment inks only on the sheet — is a review rule, because the rail cannot be added to the contrast test's ground list. One item is not styling: the FF&E thumbnail changes the query and the row's markup, and the empty case has to be as good as the filled one. Tokens revert in one commit; the thumbnail does not — once a line can show an image, taking it away is a product change.

    DIRECTION C · The Dark Desk

    Direction C — The Dark Desk

    Canon D4 says depth is value contrast, and the product spends it almost nowhere in the working shell: the five charcoal grounds the contrast test names are the mobile bar, the mobile sheets, the sub-1180 log strip and the two client-preview banners — so the only charcoal a designer meets above 1180px is a preview of what the client sees.

    C takes D4's own mechanism to its conclusion. The chrome goes charcoal and the paper stays paper: the desk is a dark desk with one lit sheet on it, the spine and margin are the desk showing beside the document, and the drawer is a well cut one step deeper still. One warm clay rule marks every edge where the sheet meets the desk. Nothing on the sheet itself changes.

    The scope of the inversion. Four surfaces go charcoal: the Studio Drawer, the DocSpine, the MarginRail, and the desk route's ground. Library, People and the ledger sheets keep paper and receive only the dark drawer along the bottom edge, because the drawer is the one piece of chrome that crosses every route.

    What stays identical

    Every route, component, act, label and piece of information architecture. The greeting, the three acts and their sub-labels, both whisper notes, the roster eyebrow and its stage groups in order, one line per job and never a card, the studio index, the drawer's five doorways. The document keeps its spine with the seven marks, the running index, the in-hand block, its letterhead, red-letter zone, region heads and ledgers, its FF&E lines by room, the margin's notes and chips. C changes which ground each is printed on and nothing else — what the sheet gains is the planks, which A and B adopt identically.

    The risk taken

    The desk route inverts too. Charcoal chrome around a lit document is the easy half; the hard half is that the desk — the screen a designer opens first every morning — becomes a dark room with one sheet in it. That is C's whole argument, and the reason C can be rejected in one glance. If the desk route is refused and only the document's chrome inverts, C survives as a document treatment: the first figure below is the one to rule on.

    Recipes by surface

    Findings addressed

    The planks close the reading floor, the muted inks, the rule weights, hover, the state fill and the fourth ground in all three lanes. What C closes alone:

    F05 Room, paper and card sit inside 1.07 to 1 F06 F07 F08 F23 The one ground with value contrast is below 1180px

    C does not touch the sheet's fills, texture or imagery, so F01, F09, F10, F15, F19, F20 and F25 stay open. On the sheet, C is the planks and nothing more.

    Canon check

    • D4, five lint selectors: none tripped, and C is the strongest argument against ever needing a shadow — on a dark ground twelve stops of value lift a sheet without one. C argues against the elevation amendment; the question itself is put to the team later in this deck.
    • D1: untouched. The chrome changes colour; it does not gain a surface, a tab or a panel.
    • Typography-first: the type is untouched; what C adds is value, the mechanism D4 itself names.
    • Never a card: the roster stays lines on a sheet, and the sheet is the same object the document route already paints — one rule for an edge, no radius, not a container around each row.
    • The contrast test breaks, twice, and the fix is a required extension. Its parser is last-wins over the whole file and asserts every -ink-suffixed token against the light grounds, so a dark-register token named that way fails hard; and the scoped-override alternative is worse, because it overwrites the real token's parsed value. C must ship a dark register with no -ink suffix and a light/dark split in the parser. Separately, the base-pigment guard's exemption list goes from five files to eleven — a guard being widened, not extended.
    • The planks arrive hardcoded charcoal, and C is the lane that has to notice. The three rule weights and the state fill are values, not roles: on C's chrome they measure 1.000 to 1.159, and the fill is a 10.408 near-white blob on the desk. Every plank token needs a dark twin, not only every ink. The twins are declared in the planks and priced here.

    Keeps · Refuses · Costs

    Keeps
    The paper, at the shipped #FCFAF6. The shipped pigments, at their shipped values. Every route, act, label and region in place and in order.
    Refuses
    No type-scale change beyond the planks. No tinted paper, no darkened paper, no imagery, no texture. No night mode, no toggle, no theme switch — C is one appearance, not two. It argues against the amendment rather than asking for it.
    Scope
    Four surfaces, named above. The desk ground is painted from a desk-route token, not --bg-primary, which the route shell paints under every document route. Turning Library, People and the ledgers dark later is a second piece of work, not a token flip: People alone renders 78 pearl border-sides and 20 white card backgrounds tuned for a cream ground, and none of the three is drawn here. Price it as three to four more days and three rooms to draw. Keeping those rooms on paper is not keeping them unchanged: the drawer crosses every route, and it goes from white to #201D1B — a 16.077:1 charcoal well along the bottom edge of a cream room, on exactly the routes this paragraph says are untouched, and no figure in this deck draws it. It is the right trade and it is the price of the argument that the drawer crosses every route; the missing artifact is one Library crop.
    Costs
    Four to five days of C's own work, one day for the contrast-test parser and the exemption decision, plus the planks. The register conversion is not an ink problem: the dark twins for the three rule weights and the state fill are part of the same sweep through the same chrome components, and they are inside the four to five days. The risk is in the tail: the dark register has to be complete, or one unconverted muted ink inside the spine is a 1.505:1 line nobody can read, and one unconverted plank rule is a 1.000:1 line nobody can see — both failures are silent, not loud.

    Contrast & separation
    A's three stocks reproduce to three decimals with the v1 dock removed; B's retuned stocks gained real value against the ground, and the v3 rail fix (D41) brought the rail back above today's own 1.081:1 separation, at the price of three of the four paper inks; C's numbers are the largest in the deck, docked for stopping at the sheet's edge, with the planks' own rules now twinned for C's chrome rather than left at 1.000–1.159:1 (D42).

    A is unchanged — type, rule weight, paper stock, the tan the only thing to reject on sight.     A counts both its sweeps honestly, and its second app-wide token is scoped and priced the same way the desk ground is (D44). B's thumbnail and the open Strata number remain the long pole. C's three unmocked rooms are priced as a follow-on, and its planks' dark twins are priced inside the same 4–5 days as the ink work (D42).
    Different-product risk
    A changes no shape; the tan is rejectable and cheap to reject. B's dashboard read is genuinely fixed, leaving a taste question rather than a category error. C's inset sheet is a defensible object at 1440; at 390 it is a dark header, a white page and a dark bar — every app on the phone.

    These six numbers per lane are one critic's read, checked twice, never a vote of more than one, and never averaged into a single score.

    Where the critic and the author disagreed — and where the v3 pass closed it

    The v2 re-read raised four defects the direction docs had not yet answered. A v3 number pass closed all four; each is stated here with the disposition and the figures that settled it, rather than folded quietly into the tables above.

    • D41 — resolved in v3. B's rail moved #ECE7DF → #E8E3DB and now reads 1.098–1.106:1 against the six sheets it flanks and 1.225:1 against the untinted sheet — every one above today's 1.081:1, so B's SP-08 goes forward rather than backwards. The price is stated in full: three of the four paper inks fall under 4.5:1 on the new rail (golden hour 4.452, terracotta 4.414, sage 4.411), so the rail carries only charcoal, the muted ramp and clay-ink at 4.697, declared as a quiet stock outside contrast.test.ts's ground list.
    • D42 — resolved in v3. The planks now carry a dark twin for each rule weight and the state fill — --rule-hair-dark (1.442 / 1.447 / 1.419 on desk / rails / well), --rule-mid-dark (11.153 / 12.722 / 14.745) and --rule-strong-dark (1.720 / 1.750 / 1.735), plus a dark fill at 1.356:1 against the rails — against the untwinned charcoal's 1.141 / 1.000 / 1.159 and 1.015 / 1.000 / 1.011. C spends all four, priced inside the same 4–5 days as the ink work, because it is the same sweep through the same chrome components.
    • D44 — resolved in v3. --bg-surface is now scoped the same way A's desk ground is scoped — a --doc-surface declared on the Document tree — and A's Cost names the unscoped count that motivates it: 83 usages across 51 files, most of them portal-shell components outside the Document tree, priced as the alternative.

    RECOMMENDATION

    Planks first, A as the floor, then one visible move

    The ruling in front of the team is smaller than the deck makes it look, and the work behind it is larger. Three decisions, taken in order, cover the package.

    1 · The planks ship as one lane, before any direction

    SP-01 through SP-09 close the same findings in every lane — the reading floor, three muted inks that are three colours, three rule weights, an ink for every pigment, a state that fills, a hover that says something, a drawer with a ground, two rails you can see, and one ground under the page at every width. None of them adds a surface, moves a region or changes a label. SP-01 alone is 1,749 text-[<n>px] literals across 252 files, sized L, 4–6 days — the largest single piece of work in the package, and every lane's own figures already assume it has landed.

    2 · Direction A is the floor

    A ships next, whatever else the team decides: the section head, the three-weight rules, and the three paper stocks 1.15:1 and further apart, with the desk ground scoped to /desk rather than to --bg-primary. It is the only lane whose separations reproduce to three decimals across two critiques — the critic's own words are that A is the one lane in which no arithmetic error can be found — and the only lane that adds rank above the shared floors rather than only inheriting them. Its own work is 2–3 days on top of the planks.

    3 · Then the team picks one visible move

    The planks and A close the flatness complaint on their own terms; a visible move is a separate, optional decision. The recommendation is C's chrome — the Studio Drawer, the DocSpine, the MarginRail and the /desk route's own ground, taken dark — on three grounds: value contrast is the mechanism canon already names for the role (D4), the mobile bar has already proven the move in production at 14.46:1, and it is the one candidate that gives the desk a desk rather than another tint on the same paper. It is not free to take today: the planks now carry a dark twin of every rule and fill token, not only every ink, priced inside C's own 4–5 days rather than added to them (D42, resolved in v3), and contrast.test.ts's parseTokens still needs its light/dark split, with the exemption list's widening from five files to eleven named as the cost (D19, priced at 1 day and called non-optional).

    Two grafts from B survive either choice and should be taken regardless of which visible move wins. The charcoal letterhead band with the red-letter zone carried on it — the palest band on the document becomes the highest-contrast object on it, 12.485:1 on the stock the band actually sits on, still the strongest single answer to F09 anyone in this deck proposes. And the filled stamps: five state fills at 16–18% over the sheet with a matching -ink, the fullest execution of the plank any lane offers, with the one tight margin (damaged, terracotta-ink and sage-ink) held at 4.63:1, not the 4.51:1 v1 shipped.

    Two parts of B wait. The movement tints wait: pairwise, the six stocks still sit at only 1.000–1.007:1 — a movement is told from another movement by hue alone, not by value — even now that the rail itself is fixed (D41, resolved in v3: #E8E3DB reads 1.098–1.106:1 against the six sheets it flanks, above today's own 1.081:1, at the price of three of the four paper inks losing the rail entirely). The thumbnails wait: on the local seed, zero of six FF&E lines carry a product_id, so B's headline material move renders no thumbnails here, and nobody in this program has the one number that would say whether that is also true in production.

    The sequence

    Planks
    4–6 days for SP-01 alone, the rest folded in beside it; sequenced first, no direction ships before it. Reverts by token except the two sweeps (1,749 and 502 literals), which replace literals with tokens rather than reverting — worth keeping whichever lane wins.
    Direction A
    +2–3 days on top of the planks. High reversibility: every value is a token, reverting is one commit against :root.
    The two B grafts
    No additional estimate beyond the planks' own sizing (SP-05 is Size M); the band's token reverts in one commit, the filled-stamp departure from KIT.md:266 is already inherited by every lane.
    The visible move — C's chrome
    +4–5 days of C's own work, including the dark-twin work D42 asks for (priced inside those days, not on top of them), +1 day for the contrast-test parser. High reversibility as tokens, medium in practice: the register choice is scattered through the chrome components.
    Or, in full, Direction B
    +4–6 days of B's own work in place of C's chrome, gated on the open Strata product_id count before F15 can be ruled on. Medium reversibility: tokens revert, the thumbnail does not.

    What this recommendation refuses

    • A three-day reading of the package. SP-01 alone is 4–6 days, it is the plank that answers the actual complaint, and every lane's figures are worthless until it lands.
    • B's tints as the signature. The retune that rescued B's signature (1.001:1 → 1.081–1.088:1 against the ground) is real, and the v3 pass fixed the rail it drove backwards — #E8E3DB now reads 1.098–1.106:1 against every sheet it flanks, above today's 1.081:1 (D41, resolved in v3). What remains true is that pairwise, stock to stock, the six still sit at only 1.000–1.007:1: a movement is told from another movement by hue alone, not by value. The band and the filled stamps are taken regardless; the tints wait.
    • F15 before the production count. Locally zero of six FF&E lines carry a product_id; on that shape B's headline material move renders nothing, and the ruling should wait on the one query nobody in this program has run.
    • C's register before the dark twins are built. The planks now declare a dark twin for every rule weight and the state fill, priced inside C's own 4–5 days (D42, resolved in v3) — ship those, not the untwinned hardcoded charcoal that still measures 1.141 / 1.000 / 1.159 on C's own desk / rails / well.
    • Any shadow before the CSS gate exists. The amendment's real cost is a CSS-level gate that does not exist yet — globals.css is linted by nothing today — not the lint change its first draft claimed. Close R72's dead exception and build the gate first; decide the token second.

    QUESTIONS

    Eleven things we need answered before anyone builds

    Every card below carries the numbers that bear on it and closes with the question itself. Nothing here is a recommendation restated — section 12 already made those; this section is what the team has to rule on to make them real.

    01 · Direction · needs a ruling

    Does Direction A ship as the floor under whichever visible move the team picks?

    A is the only lane whose stock separations reproduce exactly across two critiques — paper→rail 1.177, rail→desk 1.173, paper→desk 1.381 — and the only lane that adds rank above the shared planks: a five-step Playfair scale, three rule weights spent on rank, an 18px job name against a 14px need line. Its own work is 2–3 days, on top of the planks. The one item that was open — --bg-surface resolving 83 times across 51 files outside the Document tree, priced nowhere in A's Cost — is closed in v3: it is now scoped as a --doc-surface on the Document tree, the same way the desk ground is scoped, and the 83/51 count is named as the priced alternative (D44).

    We ask: does A ship as the floor now that both of its app-wide tokens are scoped and priced?

    02 · Direction · needs a ruling

    After A, does the team take C's chrome, B's material, or neither?

    The v2 scorecard has C ahead of B on four of six axes (contrast, still-Patina, canon fit each by one to two points) and behind on cost & reversibility by a point; B is the safer, cheaper move and C is the larger, riskier one. Section 12's recommendation is C's chrome, now that D42 (a dark twin for every plank token, not only every ink) is priced — the twins are declared in SP-03 and spent by C inside the same 4–5 days — and D19 (the contrast.test.ts parser split) is priced at 1 day and called non-optional.

    We ask: which visible move, if any, follows A — and does the team want it priced before or after the planks land?

    03 · Scope · needs a ruling

    Accept A's desk ground #E0D6C4 scoped to /desk, or keep the desk white and take only the paper and rail stocks?

    The tan is the single move A names as its own risk — a team can reject it on sight after three years of one cream. It is already scoped to the desk route, not to --bg-primary: repointing the app-wide token instead would carry /library, /people and every ledger sheet tan with it, priced at +2–3 days and three rooms to draw before ruling. If the ground is refused outright, A's two rail stocks (paper→rail at 1.177:1) still open the document's three columns on their own.

    We ask: accept the tan on /desk, keep the desk white and take only the rail stocks, or price the app-wide repoint first?

    04 · Amendment · needs a ruling

    Close R72's dead exception and build the CSS gate D4's own text asks for, before deciding whether to admit one tokenized elevation?

    ESLint's D4 block covers only files: '**/*.{ts,tsx}' and never reads globals.css; no stylelint exists anywhere in this app, this workspace or the repo root. R72's filter: drop-shadow(…) at globals.css:217/223/227 ships today and trips no rule, on a .folio-face class that zero .tsx files reference — dead CSS carrying a live exception. apps/designer-portal/CLAUDE.md:19-26 asked for a stylelint rule “in your first PR” and never got one. Per D38, the amendment's own “We ask” now puts closing the dead exception and building the gate first, and admitting one token, --elevation-sheet, second. No figure to quote here — the amendment's corrected cost is zero lint change if the token is ever spent from CSS, not from a .tsx literal.

    We ask: close the exception and build the gate first, then take up the token — or leave both questions open together?

    05 · Direction · needs a ruling

    Accept B's movement told by hue alone, or drop the tints and keep the band and the stamps?

    B's six stocks now measure real value against the ground — 1.081–1.088:1, from v1's 1.001–1.020:1 — but pairwise, stock to stock, they still sit at only 1.000–1.007:1: a movement is told from the ground by value and from another movement only by hue. Reaching that value did cost the rail its own headroom, and the v2 rail went backwards — a defect the v3 pass fixed: the rail moved to #E8E3DB and now reads 1.098–1.106:1 against the six sheets it flanks and 1.225:1 against the untinted sheet, above today's own 1.081:1 (D41, resolved in v3), at the price of three of the four paper inks — only charcoal, the muted ramp and clay-ink at 4.697 can still print there.

    We ask: accept a movement told by hue alone, or drop the tints and keep only the charcoal band and the filled stamps?

    06 · Data · needs a ruling

    What is the production product_id count, and does it change the ruling on F15?

    Locally, project_ffe_items has 6 rows, 0 with a product_id; products has 21 rows, 17 with images. On that shape, B's headline material move — a 48px thumbnail on a catalog-linked FF&E line — renders zero thumbnails, and the two crops in its mock are stood in to show the treatment, not the data. Nobody in this program has the Strata figure.

    We ask: run the count before ruling on F15 — and if it is near zero, is B's answer to F15 still worth taking as written?

    07 · Scope · needs a ruling

    Does C's inversion stay at four surfaces, or extend to /library, /people and the ledgers too?

    As scoped, C inverts the Studio Drawer, the DocSpine, the MarginRail and the /desk route's own ground; the three rooms keep paper and receive only the dark drawer along the bottom edge. Extending them dark is a second piece of work, not a token flip: /people alone renders 78 pearl border-sides and 20 white card backgrounds tuned for a cream ground, priced as +3–4 days and three rooms to draw, none of them mocked in this deck.

    We ask: rooms stay paper under a dark drawer as drawn, or invert all three at +3–4 days?

    08 · Direction · needs a ruling

    Do the planks ship as one lane before any direction, at SP-01's 4–6 days?

    SP-01 alone is 1,749 text-[<n>px] literals across 252 files, sized L — the largest single piece of work in the package — and every lane's own figures (A's stocks, B's stocks, C's separations) already assume it has landed. shared-planks.md calls it “the one plank that should be sequenced before any direction ships.”

    We ask: sequence the planks as their own lane first, at 4–6 days for SP-01 alone?

    09 · Scope · needs a ruling

    Does contrast.test.ts's parseTokens get a light/dark split before C ships?

    parseTokens is last-wins over the whole file and asserts every -ink-suffixed token against the light grounds only; a dark-register token carrying that suffix would fail hard, and the scoped-override alternative C's v1 draft proposed is worse — it overwrites the real token's parsed value. C's committed fix is no -ink suffix in the dark register plus a light/dark split in the parser, priced at 1 day and called non-optional (D19). Separately, the base-pigment guard's exemption list widens from five files to eleven (D20).

    We ask: is the parser split required before C ships regardless of the visible-move ruling, and does the widened exemption list get a ruling of its own?

    10 · Defect · no owner

    Who fixes the desk's 390 overflow, and when?

    A stitching pass measured 437 CSS px of content inside a 390px viewport — 47 CSS px of overflow onto a fourth, unpainted ground (F24, severity medium). It is a layout defect, not a design question: all twelve 390 mockups in this deck are drawn with it assumed repaired, and the one plank that touches it (SP-09) only repaints the ground underneath the overflow, not the overflow itself. No direction in this deck fixes it.

    We ask: who takes F24, and does it ship ahead of, or alongside, whichever direction is ruled for?

    11 · Direction · needs a ruling

    Accept SP-06's floor at what it actually measures, 1.097:1, against its own ≥1.09:1 promise?

    SP-06 no longer names one hex: it is a rule — a hovered row takes the next stock the lane already declares — because no single value cleared 1.10:1 across every stock every direction proposes. The token this plank tried, --plank-hover-tint: #F3ECE2, measured 1.008–1.125:1 across the declared stocks and inverted direction on two of them — 1.228:1 on A's desk and 1.089:1 on B's rail, both lighter than the ground rather than darker — and a fill deep enough to clear 1.10:1 everywhere else broke the 4.5:1 ink floor: charcoal at 6% over A's desk stock reads 1.106:1 and drops A's tightest -ink to 4.137:1 on the hovered row; over B's Project stock, 1.115:1 and 4.363:1 (D43, resolved in v3). The plank now promises a floor of at least 1.09:1, not 1.10:1, and delivers exactly 1.097:1 at its tightest point — C's second sheet. Every lane clears it with a stock it already owns: A at 1.177 / 1.177 / 1.173, B at 1.108–1.116:1 with 1.225:1 on its rail, C at 1.097 / 1.141 / 1.159.

    We ask: accept the plank's 1.097:1 floor against its own ≥1.09:1 promise, or ask for a higher floor than any single value could deliver across three lanes' stocks?

    COLOPHON

    How this was made, and what it rests on

    Method, in order

    1. Scaffold and kit port. The program folder, the mock kit and its four I151 -ink tokens, the build and QA scripts ported from two earlier deck programs.
    2. Fresh captures. Twenty-two shots at 1440 and 390, taken 2026-08-28 against the local seed, signed in as designer Leah Hartwell. Twenty-two of twenty-two exist; twenty-one verified as the intended surface, one a documented, source-confirmed unreachable state.
    3. A DOM measurement script. Every visible element's computed style, read off the rendered page at /desk, /doc/<Chen Residence>, /library and /people, contrast math ported verbatim from contrast.test.ts.
    4. One audit seat. A simulated designer's eye — a senior interior designer at a Midwest studio, stated plainly wherever it speaks — walked every capture against the measurer's numbers and wrote the findings.
    5. Priors harvest. Verbatim quotes with file and line from four earlier reviews of the same surface, folded in beside the fresh findings.
    6. One author, three lanes. A single context wrote Directions A, B and C, the shared planks and the amendment together, for coherence across lanes rather than three separate voices.
    7. An adversarial critic. A fresh context, never the author, found thirty-nine defects (D01–D39) against the repo, the fresh captures and recomputed WCAG arithmetic.
    8. v2. The same author answered every defect — fix, accept, or drop with a stated reason — against the same critic's rubric.
    9. A second critique, same critic. Thirty-five of thirty-nine resolved, four partly, zero unresolved, zero disputed — and ten new defects surfaced by the revision itself (D40–D49), mostly residue of retunes that fixed one number and left its neighbor stale.
    10. A v3 number pass. Where D40–D49 asked for a printed figure to be corrected, the direction docs were updated once more; this deck quotes whatever value stood in the source files at the moment each part was written.
    11. Deck parts, build gates, QA, fact-check. Fourteen sections, each under its own character budget, each F-id and D-id checked against the research folder; a build that fails on a stray shadow, an unresolved marker, or a disallowed host; a rendered QA pass at both widths and both themes.

    The roster

    Roles, not names. Models are named where the program recorded them.
    RoleWorkModel
    Steward Booted local dev against the seed, resolved the document ids, captured the twenty-two shots at 1440 and 390, ran the DOM measurement script Sonnet
    Priors & canon digest Verbatim quotes with file and line from four earlier reviews; the D1/D4/O4/R72/I151 canon citations Haiku
    Audit seat One simulated seat, walked every capture against the measurer's numbers, wrote the findings F01–F25 Opus
    Author Wrote all three directions, the shared planks and the amendment in one context, then revised all three against the critique twice (v2, v3 number pass) Opus
    Critic Fresh context, never the author; the v1 critique (thirty-nine defects) and the v2 re-read (thirty-five resolved, four partly, ten new) Opus
    Part authors The fourteen deck sections; the direction authors wrote their own sections (06–08), others were written apart from the direction author Opus · Sonnet · Haiku
    Orchestrator Planned the phases, dispatched every seat above, read every gate's output, published the deck Fable

    No seat reviewed its own work: the critic never authored a direction, and the audit seat never wrote a finding's fix. Reviewer briefs asked for every defect with a confidence and a severity, never for high-severity defects only — a severity filter depresses recall.

    The file ledger

    The program folder, one line per folder.
    RESUME.md · presentation.htmlThe program's own index and the built deck this section closes.
    research/The shot ledger, the measurement script and its output, the visual audit and the findings, the environment and id log.
    source/The ask, the specimen, the plan, the three direction documents with their v1 drafts kept beside them, the shared planks, the amendment, and the critique with its v2 re-read.
    shots/The twenty-two PNGs the steward captured, 1440 and 390, against the local seed.
    mock/The kit, the three direction stylesheets, the fourteen drawn fragments, the deck parts and their build and QA scripts, the fonts and the product crops.

    What this deck does not claim

    • No user research was run. Every finding, every quote and every “blends” comes from one simulated seat and the measurements beside it, never from a designer's own session.
    • The designer's voice throughout this deck is a simulated seat — a senior interior designer at a Midwest studio, stated plainly wherever it speaks — not a real practitioner walked through the product.
    • Every capture in this deck is the local seed, not a production account. StatusChip never rendered on this data: plan_sheets and every proposal_items row with a product_id are both empty locally, and the one shot attempted at it is a documented failure, not a verified render. The install-stage shot required lifting the project's state by RPC, not a naturally occurring row.
    • Direction B's imagery is scoped for the mock, not for the product: on the local seed, zero of six FF&E lines carry a product_id, so B's headline material move renders zero thumbnails here, and the two thumbnails in its mock are stood in to show the treatment.
    • The six-axis scorecard is one critic's, checked twice, never a vote of more than one and never averaged into a single number.
    • Nothing in this program changed the product. No migration was written, no component was edited, no route moved — every mock is CSS on a specimen, built and inspected outside apps/designer-portal.
    • The D4 amendment is a question put to the team, not a proposal this deck argues for. No mockup here illustrates it, and no direction depends on its answer either way.
